title: Influence of intercritical annealing temperature on TRIP/TWIP effect of retained austenite and tensile deformation mechanism of IQ&P steel
abstract: The aim of this study was to investigate the effects of intercritical annealing temperature on stability of retained austenite and tensile deformation mechanism of intercritical annealing quenching and partitioning (IQ&P) steels. By varying the intercritical annealing temperatures (700 °C and 750 °C), the following results were observed. The microstructure of experimental steels was examined by scanning electron microscopy, X-ray diffraction, and transmission electron microscope. With the decrease of intercritical annealing temperature from 750 °C to 700 °C, the content of retained austenite is doubled, and the microstructure is obviously refined. The mechanical properties of the test steel were tested by tensile test. The results demonstrate that the sample annealed at 700 °C showed the best product of tensile strength and elongation, which was above 34 GPa⋅% (ultimate tensile strength: 1016 MPa, total elongation: 33.5%). The fracture structure and morphology of the tensile specimens were examined to explore the key factors affecting the strength and plasticity of IQ&P steel. During the tensile process, the specimens annealed at lower temperatures maintained a better Kurdjumov-Sachs orientation relationship between the γ and α phases. In addition, the combination of a uniform distribution of microscopic stress and strain, a smaller difference in hardness between the phases and increased activation of multiple slip systems allows a greater amount of retained austenite in the low-temperature annealed specimens to be continuously subject to the transformation-induced plasticity (TRIP) and twinning-induced plasticity (TWIP) effect during the tensile process. The refinement of the microstructure and retained austenite grains could occur TRIP and TWIP effects in a more sustainable way, ultimately leading to more excellent comprehensive mechanical properties of the 700 °C annealed test steels.
journal: Journal of Materials Research and Technology

sections.heading: Introduction
paragraphs: In order to cope with the problems of energy consumption and environmental pollution, automobile steel is gradually developing toward lightweight [ 1 ]. However, conventional high-strength steel, as well as the first and second generations of high-strength steel, can no longer meet the practical requirements. Therefore, it is quite essential to research and develop the 3rd generation AHSS with both low-cost and superior comprehensive mechanical performance. Presently, the third-generation AHSS increases strength primarily through conventional methods such as precipitation strengthening, fine-grain strengthening and dislocation strengthening. In addition, the third generation of high strength steel usually introduces retained austenite. The transformation induced plasticity (TRIP) and twinning-induced plasticity (TWIP) effect of retained austenite can benefit ductility and formability [ 2 , 3 ].

Medium manganese steels containing approximately 4–12 wt% of Mn possess both high strength and excellent ductility, and are thus considered to be third-generation advanced high-strength steels with significant development potential [ 4 ]. The microstructure of medium-Mn steels is a dual-phase or tri-phase structure composed of metastable austenite and fine ferrite and/or martensite [ 5 , 6 ]. The ferrite obtained by intercritical annealing contains less carbon and manganese. The excess C and Mn can accumulate in the austenite phase during annealing. This increases the thermal stability of the retained austenite so that the steel can retain 20 to 50 vol% retained austenite at room temperature. In addition, different rolling processes lead to variations in the distribution of retained austenite and ferrite. Hot rolling followed by intercritical annealing results in retained austenite and ferrite being present in a strip-like form with an alternating distribution [ 7 ]. In contrast, cold rolling and subsequent intercritical annealing mainly produce retained austenite and ferrite in smaller equiaxed forms [ 8 ]. Although both processes can produce experimental steels with a high product of strength and elongation, most have a lower tensile strength. To achieve higher tensile strength while ensuring excellent plasticity, intercritical annealing, quenching and partitioning (IQ&P) processes are used in this study.

The traditional Q & P process adjusts the retained austenite content and stability by full austenitization and precisely controlling the quenching temperature and distribution time [ 9–12 ]. Although the Q&P has achieved some success in improving the stability of retained austenite, the TRIP effect of the retained austenite is not significant [ 11 ]. To further enhance the content and stability of retained austenite in medium manganese steel, the temperature of full austenitization is adjusted to the intercritical annealing temperature [ 13 , 14 ]. This improvement not only increases the content and stability of austenite but also promotes coordinated deformation among different phases, and significantly improves the TRIP effect [ 15 , 16 ].

As we know, high-angle grain boundaries (HAGBs) and low-angle grain boundaries (LAGBs) play a decisive role in determining the mechanical properties of the AHSS steel. Under plastic deformation conditions, HAGBs exhibit a tendency to deflect and inhibit crack propagation, leading to increased plasticity [ 17–20 ]. According to the studies of Wang et al. [ 17 ], the presence of HAGBs can change the direction of crack propagation, which is an important factor in fracture toughness. However, it should be noted that the formation of grain boundaries is influenced to a certain extent by crystallographic properties. X.L. Wang et al. discovered that different Bain variants within the same CP group are predominantly present in the form of HAGBs, while different CP groups have mainly LAGBs [ 21 ]. Further studies by Y. Dong et al. has shown that within one and the same CP group, increased formation of different variants can effectively increase the proportion of HAGBs [ 22 ]. In addition, A. Lambert-Perlade et al. observed that the LAGBs are made up of V1 and the other seven variants (V4, V8, V11&V13, V16, V21, and V24) [ 23 ]. B. Wang et al. have made an interesting discovery that small primary austenite grains (PAGs) contribute to adaptive transformation drives and reduce variant selection [ 24 ]. As the number of PAGs increased, the transition from the CP group to the Bain group became more pronounced. Y. Dong et al. have shown a significant relationship between the variant selection and the temperature of the phase transformation and the driving force [ 22 ]. Furthermore, M. Zhou et al. have conducted a study on the influence of deformation on variant selection and observed a remarkable enhancement of variant selection under higher stress conditions [ 25 ]. Therefore, it is obvious that the study of crystallographic features is of utmost importance. However, the previous studies focused mostly on variant selection has focused on bainitic and martensite steels. There are few studies that were more concerned about the effect of annealing temperature on variant selection in medium manganese steel. Hence, this study aims to explore the impact of annealing temperature on the variants, analyzing the correlation with mechanical properties while considering crystallographic characteristics.

Similar to conventional TRIP steels, retained austenite in medium manganese steel plays a crucial role during tensile deformation. It significantly enhances the overall mechanical properties of medium manganese steel through the TRIP and TWIP effects. The key factors that determine the deformation mechanism of TRIP and TWIP are manganese content and the value of stacking fault energy (SFE) [ 26–29 ]. A study by S. Zhang et al. shows that blocky retained austenite is more prone to the TRIP effect compared to thin-film retained austenite [ 2 ]. Research has shown that the retained austenite located between martensite and bainite laths exhibits higher deformation resistance due to the “stress shielding” effect of the hard martensite. In contrast, the RA adjacent to ferrite and bainitic ferrite has relatively lower stability due to its structural characteristics [ 30–34 ]. Current research generally supports the notion that the occurrence of the TRIP effect is closely related to the stability of the retained austenite. The worse the stability is, the more likely the TRIP effect is to occur [ 35–37 ]. Consequently, this study focuses primarily on increasing the stability of retained austenite while facilitating its involvement in the TRIP effect. This provides a theoretical basis for improving the overall mechanical properties of steel.

In this research, a thorough investigation was conducted to understand the impact of various intercritical annealing temperatures on stability of retained austenite and tensile deformation mechanism of IQ&P steel. To do this, advanced technologies such as electron backscatter diffraction (EBSD), transmission electron microscopy (TEM), X-ray diffraction (XRD), and chemical reaction kinetics simulation software were used. In addition, the TRIP/TWIP effect of retained austenite and its effect on the mechanical properties of steel were studied by tensile testing.

sections.heading: Development of IQ&P steel
paragraphs:
The chemical composition of the steel with a medium manganese content used in this study can be found in  Table 1 
                         . A 50 kg ingot was cast in a vacuum induction furnace and then hot-forged into a 150 × 50 mm billet. The billet was then allowed to cool naturally to room temperature. To achieve uniformity, the billet was heated at 1250 °C for 2 h, followed by hot rolling. The initial rolling temperature (IRT) was set at 1100 °C, while the final rolling temperature was precisely controlled in the range of 850 °C–900 °C, resulting in a final hot rolled plate thickness of 15 mm.

The Gleeble 3500 thermal simulation system was used to calculate the phase transition temperature. The thermal simulation samples selected had a diameter of 6 mm and a length of 70 mm. The samples were first heated at a rate of 10 °C/s to 850 °C and held at this temperature for 10 min for austenitization. Subsequently, the thermal expansion curve is obtained by rapid cooling to room temperature at a cooling rate of 20 °C/s. The temperature of the phase transition point was determined from the thermal expansion curve by the tangent method, as shown in  Fig. 1 
                         (a and b). Then, the volume fraction of different phases and the chemical composition of austenite at different annealing temperatures were calculated by thermal calculation software based on the Thermo-Calc software, which is equipped with the TCFE11 database (as shown in  Fig. 1 (c and d)). The quenching temperatures under different annealing conditions were determined by the constrained carbon equilibrium (CCE) model ( Fig. S1 ). Based on these findings, The rolled steel strips were cut perpendicular to the rolling direction (Size: 12mm × 12mm × 160 mm, and then perform IQ&P heat treatment, as schematically shown in  Fig. 1 (e). The samples were heated up to 700 °C/750 °C for 15min for intercritical annealing and then quenched in a salt bath furnace to 170/180 °C for 15 s. Finally, the samples were placed in a salt bath furnace at 400 °C for 360 s, and then the samples were quenched to room temperature with the quenching rate of 20 °C/s, whereby the samples intercritical annealed at 700 °C and 750 °C were designated IA700 and IA750, respectively.

The microstructure was characterized by scanning electron microscopy (SEM, ThermoFisher/Apreo S HiVac, USA) and optical microscopy (OM, Leica/DM2700 M, Germany). The preparation of metallographic specimens adhered to a stringent procedure: the specimens were coarsely ground, finely ground (3000#), and polished. After these steps, the specimens were etched for a brief period (10s–15s) using 4 vol% nitric acid-alcohol solution at room temperature to reveal the microstructure.

The Electron Backscatter Diffraction technique (EBSD, oxford/Symmetry, UK) was employed to meticulously characterize the microstructural morphology, crystallographic orientation relationships, and phase distribution of the samples. Sample preparation for EBSD requires coarse grinding and fine grinding (2000#) first, followed by electropolishing in a solution of 4 vol% perchloric acid + 90 vol% alcohol at a temperature of −20 °C. The specific operating conditions involved applying a voltage of 30V for a duration of 25s–30 s. During EBSD analysis, the working voltage was set at 20 KV, the current at 13 nA, and a step size of 0.1 μm was selected. The sample tilt angle was fixed at 70° to obtain optimal analysis results.

A Transmission Electron Microscope (TEM, CF-HR/JEM-F200, Japan) equipped with an Energy-Dispersive Spectrometer (EDS, oxford/Aztec Ultim Live 100 X, UK) is suitable for observing and analyzing the microstructure and element distribution of materials. To observe the microstructure by TEM, the samples were ground to a thickness of 60 μm–80μm and then thinned with an electrolytic twin-jet polisher (Struers/TenuPol-5, Denmark) in a solution of 10 vol% perchloric acid and 90 vol% glacial acetic acid. This process occurs at a working voltage of 50V and a temperature of −20 °C to ensure the quality of the sample. During the observation stage of the transmission electron microscope, the working voltage is set to 200 kV, and the emission current is controlled between 10 μA and 15 μA to achieve optimal imaging results.

The retained austenite in the sample was quantitatively analyzed by an X-ray diffractometer (XRD, Rigaku/SmartLab SE, Japan) with a Cu-Kα radiation source. The sample preparation method of this analysis was the same as the EBSD in this study. sections.heading: Microstructure characterization
paragraphs:
As shown in  Fig. 2(a–c) and (d-e) 
                         , these images show the OM, SEM, and FCC phase IPF + BC images of IA700 and IA750, respectively. The microstructures of the samples intercritical annealed at different temperatures were ferrite, retained austenite, and martensite. In sample IA700, the proportion of ferrite and retained austenite is higher, while IA750 contains a larger amount of martensite, as depicted in  Fig. 2 (a) and (d). This difference is mainly due to the fact that more ferrite is formed in the sample when intercritical annealing at 700 °C compared to intercritical annealing at 750 °C ( Fig. 2 (b)), where ferrite has a lower content of carbon and manganese elements. The excess C and Mn are distributed to the austenite during intercritical annealing, which increases the stability of the retained austenite. During quenching, there is less transformation of retained austenite to martensite (as indicated in  Fig. 2 (c), the area ratio of retained austenite is 31.1 %.). Conversely, intercritical annealing at 750 °C leads to a lower ferrite content. The excess C and Mn in the ferrite are distributed to the austenite to a lesser extent, which leads to a reduction in the retained austenite content at room temperature (as shown in  Fig. 2 (f), the area ratio of retained austenite is 15.8%) and an increase in the martensite content. In addition, the retained austenite has a similar crystallographic orientation to the primary austenite grains (as shown in  Fig. 2 (c) and (f)), a phenomenon known as the austenite texture memory effect [ 38 , 39 ].

Due to the limitations of the EBSD technique with a step size of 0.1 μm, it is not possible to detect fine retained austenite. To obtain more accurate measurements of the volume fraction and carbon content of retained austenite, X-ray diffraction analysis was performed as described in  Fig. 3 
                         . It can be seen from the results that the volume fraction of retained austenite in the IA700 sample is significantly higher at 42.5 vol% compared to the IA750 sample. Interestingly, the carbon content in both samples is almost identical. This phenomenon can be attributed to the fact that although the austenite in the IA750 sample initially had a lower carbon content during the intercritical annealing phase, it transformed more strongly into martensite during the subsequent quenching. Consequently, the carbon content in the martensite is redistributed to the retained austenite during the partitioning stage, resulting in retained austenite with a similar carbon content to the IA700 sample.

Fig. 4 
                          shows the TEM correlation diagram of the sample.  Fig. 4  (a) and (d) show that sample IA750 has a higher dislocation density in the ferrite phase. This can be attributed to the presence of a larger amount of unstable retained austenite (γ) in the IA750 sample, which transforms into martensite (α) during the cooling process. The γ→α transformation causes a volume expansion, which leads to a lattice distortion in the surrounding ferrite. In order to compare the average width of retained austenite at different intercritical annealing temperatures, the average width measurements were performed on the retained austenite of IA700 and IA750 samples (at least 50 measurements were taken and the average value was calculated). The final measurement results show that the average width of the retained austenite in the IA700 and IA750 samples is 134.3 nm and 141.8 nm, respectively.  Fig. 4 (b–e) shows the gradual decrease in manganese content from austenite to martensite and then to ferrite. To accurately assess the differences in the element content of retained austenite at different intercritical annealing temperatures, EDS point scans were performed on different areas of the sample (as depicted in  Fig. S3 ). The results show that the Mn content of retained austenite in IA700 and IA750 samples is about 8.60 wt% and 7.85 wt%, respectively. It is generally known that the stability of retained austenite in hot-rolled manganese steel is primarily influenced by the carbon and manganese content and the size of the austenite phase [ 30 , 40 ]. Based on the aforementioned results, it can be concluded that the IA700 sample exhibits a 1.35 wt% higher Mn content in the retained austenite compared to the IA750 sample and also demonstrates a smaller size. Furthermore, X-ray diffraction (XRD) analysis revealed that the carbon content in the retained austenite of IA700 and IA750 samples was 0.52% and 0.51%, respectively (as shown in  Fig. 3 ). Therefore, the stability of the retained austenite in the IA700 sample is better than in the IA750 sample.

sections.heading: Mechanical properties
paragraphs:
Fig. 5 
                          shows the tensile properties of the samples at different intercritical annealing temperatures. From  Fig. 5  (a), it can be seen that both IA700 and IA750 exhibit continuous yielding behavior without any significant difference in yield strength. However, IA700 has a lower ultimate tensile strength (UTS, UTS = 1016 MPa) than IA750 (UTS = 1572 MPa), but its total elongation (TE, TE = 33.5%) is significantly higher than that of IA750 (TE = 16.7%). When evaluating the comprehensive mechanical properties of the two experimental steel samples using the product of strength and elongation (PSE, PSE = UTS × TE). Obviously, the PSE value of IA700 (PSE = 34.04 GPa·%) is significantly higher than that of IA750 (PSE = 26.25 GPa·%). Furthermore, extensive literature research was conducted to collect data on the mechanical properties of medium manganese steels (the Mn content is 5 wt%) and compare them to the medium manganese steel used in this study, as illustrated in  Fig. 5 (c). Compared to the steels tested in this study, most 5Mn steels have lower comprehensive mechanical properties. Steels with higher comprehensive mechanical properties typically have lower yield strengths (YS) (YS < 650 MPa), and are typically produced through cold or warm rolling processes. The PSE is a measure of energy absorption capability, or toughness, which is an important material selection parameter for automotive grade steels. Another important material parameter is YS, which determines structural integrity and fatigue properties. Overall, the 5Mn steels developed in this study provide an optimal balance between PSE and YS and are simpler to produce. The results demonstrate that the medium manganese steel employed in this study exhibits competitive performance when compared to other medium manganese steels.

The analysis of the work-hardening behavior of tensile specimens is an effective approach to understanding the hardening mechanism of IQ&P steel. From  Fig. 5 (b), it can be seen that the work-hardening rate curves of IA700 and IA750 samples can be divided into four different stages. In the initial stage (Stage I), the work-hardening rate exhibits a sharp decrease, which is primarily due to plastic deformation [ 41 ]. With increasing strain, the work-hardening rate shows considerable fluctuations (stage II), which is due to the discontinuous TRIP effect in the unstable retained austenite at lower strains [ 29 ]. If the strain increases further, the work-hardening rate stabilizes (stage III). The work hardening rate of IA750 gradually decreases, while the work hardening rate of IA700 specimen remains almost constant. In addition, the work hardening rate of the IA750 exhibits larger fluctuations in this stage. This can be attributed to the close correlation between the work hardening rate and the stability of the retained austenite. The more stable the retained austenite is, the slower the work hardening rate decreases, which enables a sustained TRIP effect and lower fluctuations.

The necking phenomenon begins when the material's rate of work hardening reaches equilibrium with the local true stress. This stage is the fourth stage of material work hardening (stage Ⅳ). Before necking occurs, the material exhibits a strong hardening capacity, sufficient to counteract the stress increase due to the reduction in cross-sectional area. However, once the work hardening ability of the material begins to weaken, the necking phenomenon becomes an inevitable result. In contrast, under the same conditions, the rate of work hardening of the IA700 specimen decreases more gently. This difference reveals a more significant tendency towards necking for the IA700 specimen compared to the IA750 specimen during the tensile process.

The microstructure of the IA700 specimens was significantly plastically deformed, resulting in more tortuous cracks at the fracture surfaces. This increased energy consumption during crack propagation, effectively preventing further crack propagation. The remarkable effect can be attributed to the higher retained austenite and ferrite content in the IA700 specimens, particularly the increased stability of retained austenite. Consequently, IA700 exhibits a stronger inhibition of crack propagation. In addition, the microscopic voids indicated by the red circles in  Fig. 6  were detected. Because of the differences in hardness between the two phases, these microscopic voids are primarily found at the boundaries of the lath structures in IA700 specimens. In the IA750 specimens, in addition to microscopic voids formed at the lath boundaries, voids were also detected inside the martensite/austenite island. This occurrence is primarily due to the uneven distribution of carbon content within the martensite/austenite islands. Retained austenite in the region with lower carbon content exhibits lower stability, leading to the TRIP effect under lower strain conditions and the formation of harder martensite. The significant difference in hardness from the surrounding regions causes microscopic voids to form.

Fig. 7 
                          shows the fracture morphology images of IA700 and IA750. The fracture surfaces of the IA700 tensile specimens exhibit a significant number of dimples, some of which are large and deep (as shown by the yellow arrow in  Fig. 7 (a–c)). This observation indicates that the IA700 tensile specimens fractured primarily through plastic means. However,  Fig. 7  (d) shows a clear contrast compared to IA700, as the fracture surfaces of IA750 show a clear increase in the number of quasi-cleavage fractures and cracks (shown by the red dashed line and the blue arrow in  Fig. 7 (d)). In addition, the dimples shrink in size and number. This indicates that a combination of ductile and cleavage fracture occurred during the fracture of the IA750 tensile specimens.

Fig. 8 presents the EBSD characterization of different locations on the fracture surface.  Fig. 8(a–d), (b, e) 
                         , and (c, f) show the EBSD results for the necking region (N), the transition region between the fracture and the uniformly strained region (T), and the uniformly strained region (U), respectively. A schematic diagram illustrating these regions can be found in  Fig. S4 . The figure clearly shows that the IA700 sample's microstructure in the N, T, and U regions is elongated along the tensile loading direction, indicating that it has high plasticity (as shown in  Fig. 8 (a–c)). Conversely, the N to U region of IA750 exhibits a slight plastic deformation. This discrepancy indicates that IA700 has a higher ductility compared to IA750. To gain a better understanding of how different grains influence crack propagation, the microstructure within the white boxes in  Fig. 8 (a) and (d) were magnified so that specific grains and their corresponding Schmid factors (SF) could be identified at the crack tip (as highlighted in  Fig. 8 (g–i)). The observed results show that the crack becomes blunted as it propagates to grains with a higher Schmid factor (SF > 0.45). To investigate the role of retained austenite in plasticity during tensile deformation at different intercritical annealing temperatures, the retained austenite in the N, T and U regions was statistically analyzed ( Fig. S5 ). Retained austenite was not found in the N region of either the IA700 or IA750 specimen. In the T and U regions, the IA700 samples had retained austenite contents of 0.3% and 1.6%, respectively, whereas the IA750 samples retained austenite contents of 2.3% and 5.8%, respectively. The retained austenite content gradually increased in both samples with distance from the fracture. Although the IA700 specimens initially had twice the retained austenite content of the IA750 specimens and the retained austenite in the IA700 specimens showed better stability, the retained austenite content after fracture was significantly lower in the IA700 specimens than in the IA750 specimens. This suggests that a greater proportion of retained austenite in the IA700 specimens is involved in the TRIP effect during the tensile process, as explained in detail in the sections that follow.

Fig. 9 
                          shows TEM images of the experimental steel after tensile deformation. It can be observed that the dislocation density in both samples gradually increases as the distance to the fracture decreases. In the U region of the IA700 specimen, significant plastic deformation can be seen in the lath structure, which is consistent with the observations in  Fig. 8 . The interfaces between the laths in the T region blur, indicating a strong deformation of the lath structure [ 58 ]. In  Fig. 9 (a), the N region of the IA700 sample shows an almost indistinguishable interface between the laths. In addition, high-density dislocations form in this region, forming a large number of dislocation cells. These dislocation cells have a higher dislocation density near the edges and a lower density in their center. The abundance of dislocation cells indicates a greater degree of ductility in the material. Furthermore, twinning was observed around the dislocation cells, which is consistent with the results of C. Song et al. [ 59 ]. The formation of twins in the N regions of the IA700 specimen may facilitate the activation of additional slip systems and promote plastic deformation [ 60 ]. In addition, twins can compete with dislocations to improve the strength of the sample [ 61 ]. In sample IA750, the dislocation density increases significantly from U to T, but no significant plastic deformation is observed. The width of the laths remains largely unchanged, and the boundaries of the laths in the T region remain clear. In the N region, the interfaces between the laths become somewhat blurred.

sections.heading: Variation selection
paragraphs:
Previous studies have demonstrated that the variant selection has a decisive influence on the mechanical properties of steel. Therefore, it is necessary to investigate the influence of variant selection on the mechanical properties of IQ&P steel. Within a single-parent austenite, it is possible to form 24 variants, and the 24 variants can be divided into 4 CP groups or 3 Bain groups, as shown in  Table S1  [ 2 ].  Fig. 10 
                          shows representative microscopic images of the parent austenite grains selected from the EBSD maps of IA700 and IA750. The illustrations in  Fig. 10 (a) and (d) represent the (100) pole figures of the two parent austenites. The (100) pole figures show the Kurdjumov-Sachs orientation relationship (K–S OR) between the face-centered cubic and body-centered cubic phases. However, the (100) pole figure of IA750 shows a slight deviation from the standard (100) pole figure, which is primarily due to the significant lattice distortion in the BCC phase of the IA750 sample [ 62 ], as shown in  Fig. 4 .  Fig. 10  (b, c) and (e, f) show the CP and Bain diagrams of the parent austenite in IA700 and IA750, respectively. The CP1 group dominates the IA750 sample, whereas the CP groups in IA700 are more evenly distributed throughout the parent austenite. In addition, each CP group contains 2–3 Bain groups, and the Bain groups in the IA700 sample are smaller and more evenly cross-distributed with high-angle grain boundaries between different Bain groups. X.L. Wang et al. [ 21 ] discovered that during crack propagation, different Bain boundaries are more prone to deflection, increasing the plasticity of the tested steel. Consequently, the IA700 specimen is more effective in suppressing crack propagation.

To provide a clearer description of the patterns of variant selection, a statistical analysis of variant fractions on at least 10 original austenite grains was performed, as depicted in  Fig. 11 
                         . The results show that IA700 has a more uniform distribution of variants, whereas in IA750, the CP1 group predominates, aligning with the findings presented in  Fig. 10 . This consistency indicates that the selected parent austenite grains are representative and dependable. It is worth noting that IA700 does not exhibit significant variant selection, and the variants in each CP group are relatively small and exhibit a cross-distribution, resulting in increased boundaries between CP groups. H. Terasaki et al. [ 63 ] found that the boundaries between different CP groups can cause minor local changes in crack propagation, which helps to inhibit crack propagation.

sections.heading: Austenite growth kinetics and element partitioning based on kinetic simulation
paragraphs:
The dimensions of the retained austenite and ferrite lamellae were measured by TEM experiments and resulted in an average thickness of 300 nm. Accordingly, a single-cell planar geometric model with a thickness of 300 nm was constructed. In this model, the austenite is 1 nm thick and located on the left side of the ferrite, with a movable interface between the two, as shown in  Fig. S6 .  Fig. 12 
                          illustrates that the retained austenite has higher concentrations of C and Mn under the same intercritical annealing time conditions, whereas the concentration of Al is lower. This phenomenon is due to the formation of ferrite during intercritical annealing, which has very low concentrations of C and Mn. The supersaturated C and Mn are redistributed into the austenite. Conversely, because Al is involved in ferrite formation, it is more likely to aggregate in ferrite.

At a time of 10 −5  s, in steels with two different intercritical annealing temperatures, the concentration of C in ferrite decreases gradually from the interior of the ferrite to the interface. The carbon content of austenite rises, and the distribution becomes more uniform, indicating that C is partitioned from ferrite to austenite through the interface. At different temperatures and 0.1s of intercritical annealing time, the carbon is evenly distributed in both the austenite and the ferrite. Moreover, at any given IA time, the C concentrations in austenite are always much higher in IA700 steel than in IA750 steel. This is due to increased ferrite formation in IA700 steel, which results in a large amount of supersaturated C partitioning into austenite.

At intercritical annealing times till 0.1 s, the Mn and Al concentration profiles in both ferrite and austenite remain nearly at the average Mn and Al content of the steel; this indicates no Mn and Al partitioning occurs. However, at the interface between the two phases (0.1 s < t < 10 4  s), there is a clear concentration gradient of Mn and Al. This difference is caused by the different diffusion rates of Mn and Al in austenite and ferrite. With increasing intercritical annealing time, the distribution of Mn and Al in the retained austenite gradually becomes uniform, and the effect is even more pronounced in the intercritical annealing simulation at 750 °C. Moreover, when the intercritical annealing time is greater than 10 s, the concentration of Mn in austenite of IA700 steel is always much higher than that of IA750 steel, while the concentration of Al in austenite is the inverse.

The TEM + EDS characterization of samples IA700 and IA750 was performed, as shown in  Fig. 13 
                         . The results show that the distribution of Mn elements in the retained austenite of the IA750 sample is significantly more uniform compared to the IA700 sample, which is consistent with the results of the DICTRA simulations (Due to the low temperature and short time in the quenching and partitioning process, and the slow diffusion of Mn element content, the influence of this process is ignored.). The investigations carried out by X. Tan et al. showed that the uniform distribution of the stable elements in the retained austenite plays a decisive role in the TRIP effect [ 15 ]. In the IA750 samples, the distribution of the Mn elements shows a significantly higher degree of uniformity. Consequently, the TRIP effect in retained austenite only occurs when similar strain levels. This concentrated TRIP effect leads to variations in the work-hardening rate (as shown in  Fig. 5 ) and reduces the distribution of strains over the different microstructures. In contrast, the distribution of the Mn elements in the IA700 samples is non-uniform. This leads to continuous TRIP effects in the retained austenite at different strain levels, reducing stress concentration in localized regions. Throughout 10 4  s–10 5  s, the interface moves toward the austenite direction. This is due to the peak in austenite content during this stage. As there is still a concentration gradient of Mn within the austenite, continued intercritical annealing causes the redistribution of manganese atoms within the austenite to seek chemical equilibrium. This process drives the migration of the interface towards the austenite side [ 64 ].

The integrated analysis indicates that when the holding time is less than 10 4  s, the interface between austenite and ferrite continuously migrates towards the ferrite side. However, when the holding time exceeds 10 4  s, the interface begins to shift towards the austenite side. Notably, during the isothermal treatment at 750 °C, regardless of the duration of the holding time, the interface between austenite and ferrite always remains to the right of the 700 °C isothermal. This phenomenon indicates that less austenite is formed during intercritical annealing at 700 °C. The decrease in austenite content implies a corresponding increase in ferrite content. With the elevation of ferrite content, a significant amount of carbon and manganese elements are redistributed from ferrite to austenite, enhancing the thermal stability of austenite. Therefore, more retained austenite is retained at room temperature.

Sample IA700 shows clear twinning, while the other sample does not show this phenomenon. Before deformation, the GNDs in IA700 steel were slightly lower than in IA750 steel, mainly due to a higher ferrite content in the IA700 specimens. After deformation, both specimens showed a gradual increase in GNDs from the U to the N regions. The GNDs in the U region of the IA700 specimen reached 27.98 × 10 14 /m 2 , and the maximum peaked at 30.03 × 10 14 /m 2 . In contrast, the GNDs in the U region of the IA750 specimen were only 17.68 × 10 14 /m 2 , and the maximum peaked peaking at 28.22 × 10 14 /m 2 . It can be found that geometrically necessary dislocations of the IA700 specimen is higher than that of IA750 in all regions after deformation, and there is little variation in the dislocation density between regions. This phenomenon could be due to the significant plastic deformation in the IA700 specimen during tension, which resulted in the generation of a large amount of GND to sustain the grain bending caused by non-uniform plastic deformation.

To further investigate the differences between the two specimens, a statistical analysis of the K–S orientation deviations was performed. The N region of the specimens was almost completely subjected to TRIP effects after tensioning, so no statistical analysis of the K–S orientation deviations in this region was performed ( Fig. 15 (b)). It can be observed that the K–S orientation deviation of less than 15° between the FCC phase and the BCC phase is significantly higher for the IA700 sample than for the IA750 sample. The variation in K–S orientation deviations is related to the deformation and twisting of the FCC and BCC phases during tension. The smaller orientation deviations indicate more pronounced stress-strain transfer and coordination between the two phases [ 79–82 ].

To further investigate the strain transfer phenomenon between the hard and soft phases, this study conducted high-resolution microscopy observations and geometric phase analysis (GPA) on ferrites at different locations in the IA700 specimens ( Fig. S7 ). The study found that the ferrite distributed between martensite experienced significantly lower strains than the ferrite located within the ferritic phase. This difference is primarily due to the hard phase's higher hardness, which protects the adjacent soft phase from external stress and strain [ 72 ]. It can be seen in  Fig. 9  that the dislocation density in the ferrite of each region of the IA700 sample is higher than that of the IA750. The increased dislocation density in ferrite will reduce the hardness difference between it and the surrounding hard phase, which is beneficial to the propagation of stress-strain and enhances the TRIP effect of retained austenite, to achieve continuous and uniform plastic deformation [ 83 ].

Fig. 16 
                          shows the Schmidt factor diagrams of a representative pristine austenite grain in the T and U regions of the tensile specimens. In the figure, the colors from yellow to red represent increasing Schmid factors, while the blue and green arrows indicate the slip planes and slip directions of the {110}<111> slip system, which were determined using MTEX and MATLAB. The experimental results show that most of the slip surfaces and slip directions in IA700 specimens are parallel to the lath direction. In the IA700 specimen there are slightly more slip planes and slip directions parallel to the lath direction in the T region compared to the U region. In contrast, the slip planes and slip directions in the IA750 specimens are more randomly distributed. This indicates that the {110}<111> slip system is more strongly activated in the IA700 specimens compared to the IA750 specimens [ 84 ]. The activation of the primary slip system contributes to the increase in dislocation sources and dislocation density [ 85 ]. Therefore, the dislocation density in IA700 after stretching is significantly higher than that in IA750 ( Fig. 15 ). Since there are more slip planes and slip directions parallel to the lath in the primary slip system of IA700, there is also a higher density of dislocations sliding along the lath boundaries, resulting in a larger average free path for dislocations.

It was found that IA700 has better retained austenite stability than IA750 and an austenite content 17.6% higher by volume than IA750. However, in the study conducted in Section 2.3, an interesting phenomenon was discovered: the retained austenite in the after-stretching IA700 specimens was significantly lower than that in IA750. This indicates that the TRIP effect is significantly better in IA700 than in IA750. Therefore, it is assumed that the occurrence of the TRIP effect is connected to both the distribution of microscale stresses and strains during the stretching process as well as the stability of retained austenite. During stretching, the deviation angle of the K–S orientation relationship between the FCC and BCC phase of the IA700 sample is smaller. They also contain fewer martensite areas. These factors facilitate the transfer of stress and strain and lead to a more uniform strain distribution in the micro-region. This phenomenon has been confirmed in the study of A. Dutta et al. [ 86 ]. In addition, the increased activation of the {110}<111> slip system in the IA700 specimens promotes the occurrence of uniform plastic deformation. The distribution of micro-scale stress and strain is more uniform, and the activation of multiple slip systems is enhanced, which finally makes the TRIP effect of retained austenite continue to occur. Consequently, the IA700 specimens can maintain a plasticity level of 33.5% while achieving a strength of over 1000 MPa. This improvement increases the overall mechanical performance of the steel (PSE = 34.04 GPa%).

sections.heading: Conclusions
paragraphs:
This study focuses on IQ&P steel and aims to investigate the influence of intercritical annealing temperature on its stability of retained austenite and tensile deformation mechanism. Through thorough experimentation and analysis, the following conclusions were drawn: 
                         
                            1) 
                            In the IQ&P process, the annealing temperature plays a decisive role in determining the properties of the retained austenite. It was found that the IA700 specimens had twice the retained austenite content compared to IA750. The stabilizing elements C and Mn in the retained austenite are also increased to varying degrees in IA700. In addition, the non-uniform distribution of C and Mn in the IA700 specimen resulted in a continuous TRIP effect in the residual austenite at different strain levels. 
                         
                         
                            2) 
                            The SFE of the retained austenite in the IA700 specimen exceeds 18 mJ/m 2 , indicating activation of the TWIP effect within the retained austenite. This phenomenon causes the formation of deformation twins, which can effectively redirect crack propagation while absorbing significant energy. As a result, this energy absorption mechanism contributes to the enhanced resistance to fracture in the sample. 
                         
                         
                            3) 
                            During the tensile process, different regions near the fracture surface of the IA700 specimens show a more favorable K–S orientation relationship between the FCC and BCC phases. This improved orientation relationship enhances the transfer of stress and strain between the two phases and results in more uniform plastic deformation. In addition, the IA700 specimens activate a higher number of {110}<111> Slip systems. The activation of these slip systems improves the ability for uniform plastic deformation and leads to a significant increase in both dislocation sources and dislocation density. 
                         
                         
                            4) 
                            The combination of a uniform distribution of microscopic stress and strain, a smaller difference in hardness between the phases and increased activation of multiple slip systems allows a greater amount of retained austenite in the IA700 specimens to be continuously subject to the TRIP and TWIP effect during the tensile process. This significantly improves the overall mechanical properties of IQ&P steel (PSE = 34.04 GPa%).
